question: Describe a time a small oversight or error had (or could have had) major implications. How did you catch or correct it?

raiseTranscript.text: I was updating a config file for a new feature and almost used the prod endpoint instead of staging. I caught it during a final diff before commit.
What prompted the second check?
My mentor had flagged similar issues in code review the week before, so I started running a quick grep for 'prod' on every config change.
What was the outcome?
No incident. I added the grep step to our team checklist and it caught two more cases from other juniors.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time a small oversight or error had (or could have had) major implications. How did you catch or correct it?
Role: new grad on feature team
Situation: config file with prod vs staging endpoint
Action: final diff + grep habit from recent feedback
Outcome: prevented prod exposure; added to checklist
Quote: "I added the grep step to our team checklist"
Follow-up: What prompted the second check? → cited mentor feedback and turned it into habit
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned a near-miss on a config change that could have exposed production data. They described turning recent mentor feedback into a repeatable personal check and then shared the grep pattern with the team. The story stayed within individual scope yet showed clear coachability and follow-through. The concrete habit change and checklist addition demonstrate the expected level of ownership for 0-2 years experience. Biggest strength is converting feedback into a durable process improvement rather than a one-off fix.

lowerTranscript.text: I once typed the wrong date in a report and it went out to the client. My manager caught it later.
How did you prevent it from happening again?
I try to be more careful now when I copy numbers.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: junior analyst
Situation: wrong date in client report
Action: none described beyond "be more careful"
Outcome: manager caught it; no personal process change
Quote: "I try to be more careful now"
Follow-up: How did you prevent recurrence? → vague personal intent only
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate described an error that reached a client but offered no evidence of personal ownership or learning beyond a generic statement about being more careful. There was no follow-up action, checklist, or verification step shown. The story remained entirely reactive and relied on the manager to catch the issue. Biggest gap is absence of any mechanism that would reduce the chance of the same class of error recurring.

raiseTranscript.text: While reviewing a cross-team API contract I noticed a pagination default that would break when traffic doubled. It was buried in an example payload.
What made you look that closely?
I had seen a similar default cause an outage on my prior team, so I wrote a small load test against the contract before sign-off.
Impact?
The owning team changed the default and added a note; two other services avoided the same problem before launch.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Role: senior on platform team
Situation: pagination default in shared API contract
Action: load test triggered by prior outage memory
Outcome: contract updated; two other teams protected
Quote: "I wrote a small load test against the contract before sign-off"
Follow-up: What made you look that closely? → prior outage pattern recognition
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate spotted a latent scaling issue inside an API contract that would have affected multiple teams. They used prior outage experience to justify an extra verification step and influenced the owning team plus two downstream services. The story shows cross-team impact and influence without authority through a concrete technical check. Biggest strength is turning individual scrutiny into preventive leverage for others.

lowerTranscript.text: I missed a field length limit in a shared schema and it caused retries in one downstream service. We fixed it in the next release.
The other team opened a ticket after their monitoring spiked.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: senior engineer
Situation: field length limit in shared schema
Action: none; discovered via external ticket
Outcome: fixed in next release; no preventive action described
Quote: "The other team opened a ticket"
Follow-up: How did you catch it? → purely reactive
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate allowed a schema oversight to reach another team and only learned about it through an incident ticket. No proactive verification or cross-team coordination was described. The fix was deferred to the next release without evidence of broader prevention. Biggest gap is lack of the influence and preventive habits expected at senior level.

raiseTranscript.text: One of my engineers missed updating a feature flag default during a rollout. I caught it in the pre-launch checklist I require every team member to complete with a peer.
Why the peer review step?
We had two near-misses the prior quarter; the checklist plus peer sign-off reduced flag errors to zero for six months.
How did you handle the engineer?
We added the case to our onboarding doc and I had them own the next checklist update so they internalized the control.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Role: engineering manager
Situation: missed feature flag default before rollout
Action: required peer-reviewed checklist
Outcome: zero flag errors for six months; engineer owned doc update
Quote: "I had them own the next checklist update"
Follow-up: Why the peer review step? → tied to prior near-misses and measurable reduction
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate institutionalized a peer-reviewed checklist after repeated near-misses and drove the change through team process rather than heroics. They also used the incident to develop the responsible engineer by having them own the next iteration of the control. The story demonstrates leverage through process and people development with clear before-and-after metrics. Biggest strength is turning a single oversight into durable team-level prevention while growing the individual.

lowerTranscript.text: A flag was left on in production and caused a partial outage. I reminded the team to double-check flags going forward.
We talked about it in the retro.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: engineering manager
Situation: flag left on causing partial outage
Action: verbal reminder and retro discussion
Outcome: no structural change described
Quote: "We talked about it in the retro"
Follow-up: Did the process change? → discussion only
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate responded to a production incident with a reminder and a retro discussion but showed no evidence of creating or enforcing a lasting control. The team outcome remained dependent on individual vigilance. Biggest gap is absence of leverage through process or people development.

raiseTranscript.text: During due diligence for an acquisition I noticed an inconsistency in how one product counted active users. It was a footnote in the data room.
Why did you dig into that footnote?
Revenue forecasts rested on that metric; a 12% difference would have changed the earn-out structure.
What happened?
We renegotiated the deal terms and later built a unified definition that prevented similar issues in two subsequent acquisitions.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Role: VP / exec
Situation: active-user definition inconsistency in acquisition data room
Action: flagged metric discrepancy against revenue model
Outcome: renegotiated terms; created unified definition used in later deals
Quote: "We renegotiated the deal terms"
Follow-up: Why did you dig into that footnote? → linked directly to financial model and earn-out risk
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate identified a small definitional inconsistency that carried material financial implications for an acquisition. They connected the detail to the broader deal structure and drove both an immediate term adjustment and a reusable definition across future deals. The story shows strategic judgment and long-term organizational leverage rather than isolated heroics. Biggest strength is converting a single data-room observation into durable M&A process improvement.

No evidence of personal scrutiny or preventive controls at the deal stage. Biggest gap is missing strategic ownership of detail-level risk in high-ambiguity decisions.
